ssh.name: OpenSSH server
ssh.what: The SSH server lets you open a secure remote shell and copy files to this machine.
ssh.ifFails: You lose remote access to the server. Do not stop or restart it from a session you depend on; check its logs and configuration before restarting.
ssh.details: It is the door you use to administer the server from another computer: a terminal, a file transfer tool or a deployment script connects through it. Talaia does not use SSH to manage servers, but people and automation often do. Keeping it running is what lets you get back in when something else breaks.
ssh.stop: Stopping or disabling SSH closes the remote door to the server. If you are connected through SSH, that connection ends and you may lose access completely unless you have console access from your provider. Change the configuration first and keep a working session open while you test.
problems: The connection is refused — check `systemctl status ssh` and the server firewall (for example `sudo ufw status`), and confirm the SSH port is open in the provider firewall.
The password or key is rejected — confirm the user exists, the key is in the right `authorized_keys` file and its permissions are correct; read `/var/log/auth.log` for the exact reason.
The connection times out — the server may be offline, its network may be down, or a firewall may be dropping the port; use the provider console to check the machine.

cron.name: Cron scheduler
cron.what: Runs scheduled jobs, such as backups, cleanup and maintenance tasks.
cron.ifFails: Scheduled jobs stop running until cron is started again. Check the unit logs and fix any failed job before restarting.
cron.details: Cron runs commands on a schedule: backups, cleanup, certificate checks and other maintenance. The schedule lives in each user's crontab and in files under `/etc/cron.*`. A cron job has no screen, so its output usually goes to the system log or to email.
cron.stop: Stopping or disabling cron means no scheduled job runs: backups stop, temporary files pile up and maintenance tasks are missed. Starting it again does not run the missed jobs; run the important ones by hand if needed. It is rarely safe to leave it stopped.
problems: A job does not run — check the schedule with `crontab -l` (or the file in `/etc/cron.d`), the user permissions and that the command works when run by hand.
The job runs but fails — cron uses a minimal environment; use absolute paths, set the needed variables in the crontab and read the output in the system log or the user's mail.
The service is stopped — check `systemctl status cron` and `journalctl -u cron -n 50 --no-pager`; start it only after reviewing why it stopped.

systemd-journald.name: systemd journal
systemd-journald.what: Collects the logs of the operating system and its services.
systemd-journald.ifFails: Logs stop being recorded and tools such as journalctl cannot read new entries. Restart it only if the journal is unhealthy and keep a copy of the logs first.
systemd-journald.details: systemd-journald collects log messages from the kernel, systemd and services. It stores them in the binary journal under `/var/log/journal` when persistent storage is enabled, or in memory otherwise. You read them with `journalctl`, and tools such as rsyslog may keep separate text copies. It starts early and the rest of the system expects it to be running.
systemd-journald.stop: Stopping or disabling journald stops new messages from being recorded and can leave `journalctl` with incomplete results. Existing logs are not deleted, but messages produced while it is down are lost. Do not stop it unless you are troubleshooting the journal itself; check it with `journalctl --verify` first.
problems: The journal is empty or stops growing — check `systemctl status systemd-journald`, free disk space and the output of `journalctl --verify`.
Logs disappear after a reboot — persistent storage may be disabled; check `Storage=` in `/etc/systemd/journald.conf` and whether `/var/log/journal` exists.
The journal uses too much disk — run `journalctl --disk-usage`, then lower `SystemMaxUse=` or remove old entries with `journalctl --vacuum-size=...`.
The service will not start — read `journalctl -u systemd-journald -n 50 --no-pager`; a full `/var/log` or a damaged journal file is a common cause.

systemd-logind.name: systemd login manager
systemd-logind.what: Tracks users, sessions and seats for local and remote logins.
systemd-logind.ifFails: New logins and session tracking may fail, and open sessions can be affected. Check the logs before restarting; avoid doing it while you are the only logged-in user.
systemd-logind.details: systemd-logind tracks local and remote login sessions, users and seats. It handles session cleanup, idle actions, power keys and permissions for devices such as sound cards. Desktop sessions and remote logins depend on it, and a normal SSH shell also creates a session managed by logind. It does not check passwords itself; PAM and the login program do that.
systemd-logind.stop: Stopping logind can prevent new logins and leave existing sessions without proper tracking. A connection you already have may keep working, but tools that ask logind about sessions or seats will fail. Restarting it is disruptive; prefer a reboot if it is unhealthy.
problems: New logins fail — check `systemctl status systemd-logind` and `journalctl -u systemd-logind -n 50 --no-pager`.
`loginctl` shows no sessions — check that the user session was created and that `/run/systemd/sessions` exists.
The server ignores the power button or idle settings — review `/etc/systemd/logind.conf` and the current values with `loginctl show-session <session>`.

systemd-networkd.name: systemd network manager
systemd-networkd.what: Configures network interfaces and routes on servers that use systemd-networkd.
systemd-networkd.ifFails: The server can lose network connectivity. Do not restart it remotely unless you have console access; check its configuration and logs first.
systemd-networkd.details: systemd-networkd reads `.network`, `.netdev` and `.link` files, usually under `/etc/systemd/network`, and configures interfaces, addresses and routes. It is one of several network managers on Debian; some servers use it together with systemd-resolved, while others use ifupdown or NetworkManager. Check which manager owns an interface before editing its files. Two managers trying to configure the same interface can break connectivity.
systemd-networkd.stop: Stopping systemd-networkd removes the addresses and routes it configured, so the server can lose network access. If you are connected remotely, you may not be able to start it again without console access. Validate the configuration and keep an out-of-band console ready before restarting it.
problems: The interface has no address — run `networkctl status <interface>` and check the matching `.network` file.
The default route disappeared — check `ip route` and `networkctl status`; a wrong `Gateway=` or `Address=` is a common cause.
Changes do not apply — run `networkctl reload` and read `journalctl -u systemd-networkd -n 50 --no-pager`.

systemd-resolved.name: systemd DNS resolver
systemd-resolved.what: Provides local DNS resolution and caching for the machine.
systemd-resolved.ifFails: Name resolution can fail, so services cannot find hosts or external addresses. Check /etc/resolv.conf and the resolver logs before restarting.
systemd-resolved.details: systemd-resolved provides DNS resolution and caching for the local machine. It normally listens on `127.0.0.53` and `/etc/resolv.conf` points there, so programs ask resolved instead of a remote DNS server. It can also handle `.local` names and send different domains to different DNS servers. If another resolver manages `/etc/resolv.conf`, resolved may be installed but not used.
systemd-resolved.stop: Stopping resolved can break name resolution for services, package updates and new connections. Existing connections may keep working, but new DNS lookups fail until another resolver is configured. Check `/etc/resolv.conf` and the resolver status before restarting; keep a working SSH session open.
problems: Names do not resolve — run `resolvectl status` and `resolvectl query example.com`, then check the DNS servers shown for each link.
`/etc/resolv.conf` points to the wrong place — check whether it is a symlink to `/run/systemd/resolve/stub-resolv.conf` and whether another package manages the file.
Only some domains fail — review the per-link DNS and search settings with `resolvectl status`.

systemd-timesyncd.name: systemd time sync
systemd-timesyncd.what: Keeps the system clock aligned with NTP time servers.
systemd-timesyncd.ifFails: The clock can drift, which breaks TLS, logs and scheduled jobs. Check network access to the time source; other time services may already manage the clock.
systemd-timesyncd.details: systemd-timesyncd is a small NTP client that keeps the system clock close to network time servers. It synchronizes at boot and periodically afterwards, and `timedatectl` shows its state. It is enough for most servers, but it does not serve time to other machines. Use chrony or ntp when you need a full NTP server.
systemd-timesyncd.stop: Stopping or disabling timesyncd leaves the clock free to drift; it does not change the current time immediately. Over days or weeks, drift can break TLS, logs and scheduled jobs. Start it again or make sure another time service such as chrony is managing the clock.
problems: The clock is wrong — run `timedatectl status` and check the time zone and the NTP synchronization state.
`timedatectl` says the clock is not synchronized — run `timedatectl timesync-status` and check network access to the configured servers.
Another time service is installed — check whether chrony or ntp is enabled; running two time clients can make them compete for the clock.

systemd-udevd.name: systemd device manager
systemd-udevd.what: Detects hardware and creates the device nodes services use.
systemd-udevd.ifFails: New devices, disks or network interfaces may not appear and some services cannot use hardware. Restart it only from a local console after checking the logs.
systemd-udevd.details: systemd-udevd listens for kernel device events and creates device nodes, permissions and symlinks under `/dev`. It also runs the rules in `/etc/udev/rules.d` and `/usr/lib/udev/rules.d`, which can rename interfaces or load drivers. Services that need disks, network cards or USB devices depend on udev having seen them. It starts early and normally stays in the background.
systemd-udevd.stop: Stopping udevd means new devices may not get device nodes or the expected names, and services that start later may miss hardware. Devices that are already set up usually keep working. Restarting it can disrupt device handling; do it from a local console after checking the logs.
problems: A disk or network interface does not appear — check `udevadm info --query=all --name=/dev/sdX` or `ip link`, and read `journalctl -u systemd-udevd -n 50 --no-pager`.
A device has the wrong name or permissions — inspect the rules with `udevadm test /sys/class/...` and the files under `/etc/udev/rules.d`.
The service fails — check `systemctl status systemd-udevd` and the journal; a broken rule file is a common cause.

dbus.name: D-Bus message bus
dbus.what: Carries system and desktop messages between services that use D-Bus.
dbus.ifFails: Services that depend on D-Bus can fail to start or communicate. Restarting the bus can interrupt many services; check the logs and prefer a reboot if it is unhealthy.
dbus.details: D-Bus is the message bus that lets system services and desktop programs call each other. The system bus carries messages for services such as logind and NetworkManager, while a separate session bus serves each logged-in user. Many services expect the system bus to be available at startup. It is a local communication mechanism, not a network service by default.
dbus.stop: Stopping the system bus can make services that use D-Bus fail to start or communicate, and desktop sessions will break. Some already running services may continue, but anything that tries to connect will fail. Restarting the bus is disruptive; a reboot is usually safer if it is unhealthy.
problems: A service says it cannot connect to the system bus — check `busctl list` and `systemctl status dbus`.
A desktop tool cannot reach a service — check whether the session bus is running and the user session is healthy.
The bus fails at boot — read `journalctl -u dbus -n 50 --no-pager` and check `/etc/dbus-1/system.conf` and `/etc/dbus-1/system.d`.

getty.name: Console login
getty.what: Shows a text login prompt on a local console or serial line.
getty.ifFails: You may lose the local console login. This is usually harmless on a remote server; check the serial or console configuration if you need it.
getty.details: Getty shows the text login prompt on a local console or serial line. It is how you sign in when there is no graphical session, and serial getty is often used on servers with remote console access. On a normal SSH-managed server you may never use it.
getty.stop: Stopping getty closes that console login prompt. Existing SSH sessions are not affected, and it is usually harmless on a remote server. Keep at least one console or provider recovery path before disabling all getty instances.
problems: No login prompt appears on the console — check `systemctl status getty@tty1` and the serial `serial-getty@` unit.
The serial console shows nothing — verify the baud rate and cabling, then check the unit log.
A getty restarts in a loop — read `journalctl -u getty@tty1 -n 50 --no-pager` for a failing terminal or device.

networking.name: Debian networking
networking.what: Brings up the network interfaces configured by /etc/network/interfaces.
networking.ifFails: The server can lose network connectivity. Do not restart it remotely without console access; verify the interface configuration first.
networking.details: The `networking` service is Debian's wrapper around ifupdown. At boot it reads `/etc/network/interfaces` and brings up the interfaces marked `auto`, applying addresses, routes and options. It is used by classic Debian installs; systems with NetworkManager or systemd-networkd may still have the unit but not use it for the main interface. Check which manager owns the interface before editing files.
networking.stop: Stopping `networking` runs the down commands for the interfaces it manages, so the server can lose its address and route. Over SSH, that usually means losing access until the network is restored from a console. Do not restart it remotely without a recovery path.
problems: An interface does not come up — run `ifquery --list` and `ifup --no-act <interface>` to check the configuration, then read `journalctl -u networking -n 50 --no-pager`.
The address is missing after a change — check `/etc/network/interfaces` for syntax and make sure the interface name matches.
NetworkManager and ifupdown disagree — check `systemctl status networking` and NetworkManager; disable the manager you do not use.

ifupdown.name: Network interface setup
ifupdown.what: Configures one network interface when it is brought up.
ifupdown.ifFails: That interface may stop working. Check its configuration and the unit logs, and keep console access in case the network does not return.
ifupdown.details: ifupdown provides the `ifup` and `ifdown` commands and their configuration in `/etc/network/interfaces`. The `networking` service calls them at boot, and `ifup@` units bring up individual interfaces. It is the traditional Debian network configuration system, not a daemon that keeps running. If your server uses NetworkManager or systemd-networkd, this may not manage the main interface.
ifupdown.stop: Stopping an `ifup@` unit brings down the interface it manages; stopping the `networking` wrapper affects all interfaces it started. Any remote session using that interface can be cut off. Keep console access and check the configuration with `ifup --no-act <interface>` before taking it down.
problems: `ifup` reports an unknown interface — check the interface name with `ip link` and the stanza in `/etc/network/interfaces`.
The interface comes up without an address — run `ifup --no-act <interface>` to see the commands and check the `address` and `gateway` lines.
A change does not apply — bring the interface down and up again, or restart `networking`; avoid doing it over SSH without a fallback.

rsyslog.name: Rsyslog
rsyslog.what: Writes system logs to local files and can forward them to a log server.
rsyslog.ifFails: Logs may stop reaching files or the remote collector. Check disk space and the rsyslog configuration before restarting.
rsyslog.details: Rsyslog collects messages from the system and writes them to files under `/var/log`. It can also forward them to a central server or receive messages from other machines. The `syslog` unit is a compatibility alias used by some software; rsyslog normally owns the socket.
rsyslog.stop: Stopping rsyslog stops local log files from being written and may stop forwarding. The kernel and systemd logs can still exist in the journal, but `/var/log/syslog` may stop growing. Keep it running unless another logging service has taken over.
problems: Logs stop appearing in `/var/log/syslog` — check `systemctl status rsyslog` and the configuration in `/etc/rsyslog.conf`.
The disk is full — rotate or remove old logs and check `/etc/logrotate.d/rsyslog`.
Remote logs do not arrive — check the forwarding rule, network access and the remote listener.

chrony.name: Chrony time sync
chrony.what: Keeps the clock accurate, including on machines with unstable network access.
chrony.ifFails: The clock can drift or jump, affecting TLS, logs and schedules. Check the configured time sources before restarting.
chrony.details: Chrony keeps the system clock aligned with NTP servers and can also serve time to other machines. It adjusts the clock gradually instead of jumping, which avoids breaking TLS and logs. The daemon is `chronyd`, and its configuration is `/etc/chrony/chrony.conf`.
chrony.stop: Stopping chronyd stops automatic time synchronization; the clock keeps running but drifts. Time-sensitive services can fail or reject certificates. Keep one time daemon active; do not run chrony and another NTP client together.
problems: The clock is far off — check `chronyc tracking` and the sources with `chronyc sources -v`.
No time source is reachable — check UDP port 123 and the servers in `/etc/chrony/chrony.conf`.
Chrony will not start — read `journalctl -u chrony -n 50 --no-pager` and check for another NTP daemon.

ntp.name: NTP time service
ntp.what: Keeps the system clock synchronized with NTP servers.
ntp.ifFails: The clock can drift and break TLS, logs or scheduled jobs. Check the NTP server configuration and network access before restarting.
ntp.details: The `ntp` service is the classic Network Time Protocol daemon from the NTP project. It keeps the clock synchronized and can also serve time to other machines if configured. Debian may install chrony or systemd-timesyncd instead; running more than one time daemon can cause conflicts. Check which one is active before changing the configuration.
ntp.stop: Stopping or disabling ntp lets the clock drift; other machines that used this server as a time source also lose their reference. The current time remains correct until drift accumulates. Make sure another time service is not already managing the clock before you stop it.
problems: Time is not synchronized — run `ntpq -p` and check the configured servers in `/etc/ntp.conf`.
The service will not start — check `systemctl status ntp` and `journalctl -u ntp -n 50 --no-pager`; a port conflict with chrony or timesyncd is common.
The clock is far off — check `timedatectl status` and whether another time service is running; NTP may need time to correct a large offset.

unattended-upgrades.name: Unattended upgrades
unattended-upgrades.what: Installs security updates automatically in the background.
unattended-upgrades.ifFails: Security updates may stop being installed. Check logs and free disk space, then start it again so updates resume.
unattended-upgrades.details: unattended-upgrades installs security updates automatically, usually through a daily APT timer. It reads `/etc/apt/apt.conf.d/50unattended-upgrades` and writes to `/var/log/unattended-upgrades/`. Depending on the configuration it can also remove unused packages or reboot the server. It only applies the rules you enable; it does not replace reviewing important updates.
unattended-upgrades.stop: Stopping or disabling it stops automatic security updates. The server keeps running, but known vulnerabilities stay unpatched until you install updates yourself. It is safe to stop it briefly while you change the configuration; do not leave it off unless another update system covers the server.
problems: Updates are not installed — check `systemctl status unattended-upgrades`, the timers with `systemctl list-timers`, and `/var/log/unattended-upgrades/unattended-upgrades.log`.
Packages are held back — check the origins and package lists in `/etc/apt/apt.conf.d/50unattended-upgrades` and the APT preferences.
The service fails with a lock error — another APT process is running; wait for it to finish and check `systemctl status apt-daily`.

apt-daily.name: APT daily jobs
apt-daily.what: Refreshes package lists and prepares pending updates each day.
apt-daily.ifFails: Package lists and update information can become stale. Start it again or run apt update manually; do not interrupt an upgrade already in progress.
apt-daily.details: apt-daily is a pair of systemd timers and services that refresh APT package lists and, separately, prepare upgrades. They run once a day with a random delay so many machines do not hit the mirror at once. The work is done by `/usr/lib/apt/apt.systemd.daily`, which can also start unattended-upgrades. They are not long-running daemons.
apt-daily.stop: Stopping or disabling these units stops the daily refresh and upgrade preparation. Package lists become stale and unattended upgrades may not see new security updates. You can run `apt update` manually; do not interrupt an upgrade that is already running.
problems: Package lists are old — check `systemctl list-timers 'apt-daily*'` and run `apt update` manually.
An update job is stuck — check `systemctl status apt-daily` and `journalctl -u apt-daily -n 50 --no-pager`; a lock held by another APT process is common.
Unattended upgrades do not start — check whether `apt-daily-upgrade` ran and read the logs in `/var/log/unattended-upgrades/`.

docker.name: Docker engine
docker.what: Runs containers and manages images, networks and volumes through the Docker daemon.
docker.ifFails: All containers on this server stop or become unmanageable. Check disk space and the daemon log; restarting Docker restarts its running containers.
docker.details: Docker is the service that runs every container on this server. It also keeps images, networks and volumes, so containers can start with the same data after a restart. Talaia talks to Docker through this daemon to list, start and stop workloads.
docker.stop: Stopping Docker stops all containers on this server and the panel can no longer manage them. Starting Docker again starts the containers that have a restart policy; containers without one stay stopped. Plan a short maintenance window and avoid doing it from a terminal inside a container.
problems: A container exits immediately — read `docker logs --tail 50 <container>` and check its command, environment variables and volume permissions.
The disk is full — run `docker system df` and remove unused images, stopped containers or volumes you no longer need; do not delete volumes blindly.
Docker does not answer — check `systemctl status docker` and the daemon log with `journalctl -u docker -n 50 --no-pager`; a restart restarts running containers.

containerd.name: containerd runtime
containerd.what: The container runtime Docker uses to start and stop containers.
containerd.ifFails: Docker cannot start or manage containers. Check its log and disk space; restarting containerd can disrupt every container on the server.
containerd.details: containerd is the container runtime that Docker uses to pull images, create containers and manage their lifecycle. It runs as a system service and Docker talks to it through a socket; you normally manage containers with Docker, not containerd directly. Other tools such as nerdctl or Kubernetes can also use it. It stores its state under `/var/lib/containerd`.
containerd.stop: Stopping containerd stops every container that depends on it, including Docker containers, and Docker may report errors until it returns. Starting it again does not always restart the containers; Docker or the orchestrator must do that. Plan maintenance and check disk space before restarting.
problems: Docker cannot start containers — check `systemctl status containerd`, `ctr version` and the containerd log.
The disk is full — run `ctr containers list` and `ctr images list`, then remove unused content carefully; do not delete `/var/lib/containerd`.
Containerd fails after an upgrade — read `journalctl -u containerd -n 100 --no-pager` and check `/etc/containerd/config.toml`.

apache2.name: Apache HTTP Server
apache2.what: Serves websites and web applications over HTTP.
apache2.ifFails: Websites served by Apache stop answering. Check the error log and the configuration with apachectl configtest before restarting.
apache2.details: Apache is a web server: it accepts HTTP requests and serves the sites or applications configured on this machine. It may also pass requests to another service such as PHP or a local app. If Apache is not running, visitors cannot reach those sites.
apache2.stop: Stopping or disabling Apache makes every site it serves unavailable, including HTTPS sites whose certificates are handled elsewhere. It is safe only during planned maintenance or when another web server has taken over the same ports. Check the configuration first with `apachectl configtest`.
problems: The site returns 500 — read the error log at `/var/log/apache2/error.log`; a PHP or application error is usually the cause.
The browser says the connection was refused — check `systemctl status apache2`, confirm the site is enabled and that ports 80/443 are open.
Apache will not start after an edit — run `apachectl configtest`, fix the reported file and line, then start it again.
The certificate is not renewed or the site uses the wrong one — check `certbot certificates` and the `SSLCertificateFile` paths in the site configuration.

nginx.name: Nginx
nginx.what: Serves websites and often acts as a reverse proxy for other services.
nginx.ifFails: Websites and proxied services may stop answering. Run nginx -t to validate the configuration, check the error log, then reload or restart.
nginx.details: Nginx is a web server and reverse proxy. It can serve static files directly and pass requests to application servers, often on local ports. Sites are configured in `/etc/nginx/sites-enabled` and `/etc/nginx/conf.d`, with logs under `/var/log/nginx`. After a configuration change, test it with `nginx -t` and reload rather than restart when possible.
nginx.stop: Stopping or disabling nginx makes every site and proxied application it serves unavailable. Existing connections close and visitors get a connection error. Reloading keeps downtime minimal for configuration changes; a full stop is only for maintenance or when another server takes over the ports.
problems: Nginx will not start — run `nginx -t`, fix the reported file and line, then start it again.
The site returns 502 or 504 — the upstream application is down or slow; check its service and the `proxy_pass` address.
The browser gets a connection refused — check `systemctl status nginx`, the listening ports with `ss -ltnp`, and the firewall.
Changes do not appear — run `nginx -t` and `systemctl reload nginx`; a syntax error leaves the old configuration running.

caddy.name: Caddy
caddy.what: Serves websites and obtains TLS certificates automatically.
caddy.ifFails: Websites may stop answering and certificate renewal can fail. Validate the Caddyfile and check the logs before reloading.
caddy.details: Caddy is a web server and reverse proxy that obtains and renews TLS certificates automatically. It reads a `Caddyfile`, usually `/etc/caddy/Caddyfile`, and stores certificates and state under `/var/lib/caddy`. It can proxy requests to local applications and handle HTTPS without a separate Certbot setup. Test configuration changes with `caddy validate` before reloading.
caddy.stop: Stopping or disabling Caddy makes the sites it serves unavailable, and automatic certificate renewal stops. Existing certificates remain valid until they expire. Reload Caddy for configuration changes; a full stop is only for maintenance or when another server takes over the ports.
problems: Caddy will not start — run `caddy validate --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile` and read the reported error.
HTTPS fails or the certificate is not issued — check that DNS points to this server, ports 80 and 443 are open, and read `journalctl -u caddy -n 100 --no-pager`.
The site returns 502 — the upstream application is down; check the `reverse_proxy` address and the application service.

haproxy.name: HAProxy
haproxy.what: Balances traffic between backend servers and can terminate TLS.
haproxy.ifFails: Clients cannot reach the services behind HAProxy. Check the configuration and stats, then reload carefully; a bad configuration can keep it down.
haproxy.details: HAProxy is a TCP and HTTP load balancer and reverse proxy. It accepts connections on configured frontends and forwards them to one or more backend servers, checking their health. It can also terminate TLS, add headers and expose a stats page. On a server it usually sits in front of web applications or databases.
haproxy.stop: Stopping HAProxy closes every frontend it serves, so clients cannot reach the applications behind it. Existing connections end and health checks stop. Reloading is safer for configuration changes; a full stop is for maintenance or when another proxy takes over the ports.
problems: HAProxy will not start — run `haproxy -c -f /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg` and fix the reported line.
Clients get a 503 — all backends are marked down; check the backend health and the `server` lines.
Changes do not apply — validate the configuration and reload HAProxy; a full restart drops connections.
TLS fails — check the certificate paths and permissions and the `bind ... ssl` lines.

postfix.name: Postfix
postfix.what: An SMTP mail server that sends and receives email.
postfix.ifFails: Email delivery and reception stop, and messages may be queued or rejected. Check the mail queue and logs before restarting.
postfix.details: Postfix is a mail transfer agent (MTA): it accepts mail from local programs and remote servers and delivers it to local mailboxes or other mail servers. It uses `/etc/postfix/main.cf` and `master.cf`, and keeps queued messages under `/var/spool/postfix`. On a web server it often sends notifications and contact-form mail.
postfix.stop: Stopping Postfix stops mail delivery and reception; messages from local programs may queue or fail. Mail already in the queue stays on disk. Restart only after checking the queue and logs; remote senders may retry later.
problems: Mail is not delivered — run `postqueue -p` and read `/var/log/mail.log`.
Postfix will not start — run `postfix check` and fix the reported configuration file.
Messages are deferred — check DNS, relay settings and whether the destination server is reachable.
Local mail from cron or web apps fails — check the `myhostname` and `mydestination` settings in `/etc/postfix/main.cf`.

exim4.name: Exim mail server
exim4.what: The default Debian mail transfer agent for local and outgoing email.
exim4.ifFails: Local mail delivery or outgoing email can fail and messages may queue. Check the logs and queue before restarting.
exim4.details: Exim is Debian's default mail transfer agent for many installations. It accepts local and remote mail and delivers it directly or through a smarthost (a relay server). Debian splits its configuration across `/etc/exim4/` and generates the final configuration from those files. It is often used only to send mail from cron and web applications.
exim4.stop: Stopping Exim stops local and outgoing mail delivery; messages may queue or fail. The queue remains on disk. Check the logs and queue before restarting, and remember that remote senders may retry.
problems: Mail is not sent — run `exim4 -bpc` to see the queue and read `/var/log/exim4/mainlog`.
Exim will not start — run `exim4 -bV` and check the configuration files under `/etc/exim4/`.
Messages are rejected or deferred — check the smarthost settings and DNS; `exim4 -bt <address>` tests routing.

dovecot.name: Dovecot
dovecot.what: Provides IMAP and POP3 access to mailboxes.
dovecot.ifFails: Mail clients cannot fetch mail. Existing deliveries may queue; check the logs and authentication configuration before restarting.
dovecot.details: Dovecot provides IMAP and POP3 services so mail clients can read mailboxes stored on the server. It also handles authentication and can use local system users or a database. Its configuration is in `/etc/dovecot/`, and mail is usually stored under `/var/mail` or `/home`. It does not send or receive mail itself; Postfix or Exim does that.
dovecot.stop: Stopping Dovecot closes IMAP and POP3 access, so mail clients cannot fetch or synchronize mail. Incoming mail can still be delivered to disk by the mail transfer agent. Restarting is usually safe after checking the logs; active clients reconnect.
problems: Mail clients cannot log in — check `dovecot -n`, the authentication settings and `/var/log/mail.log`.
Mailboxes are empty or missing — check `mail_location` and the permissions of the mail directory.
Dovecot will not start — read `journalctl -u dovecot -n 50 --no-pager` and check the configuration files.

fail2ban.name: Fail2ban
fail2ban.what: Bans IP addresses that repeatedly fail to authenticate to services.
fail2ban.ifFails: Brute-force protection stops and repeated attacks may not be blocked. Check its jail and log configuration before restarting.
fail2ban.details: Fail2ban watches log files for repeated authentication failures and adds temporary firewall bans for the source addresses. It uses jails defined in `/etc/fail2ban/jail.d/` and `/etc/fail2ban/jail.local`, and can protect SSH, web logins and mail. Bans are enforced through iptables, nftables or another action.
fail2ban.stop: Stopping Fail2ban removes its active bans and stops new ones from being added. The services it protects keep running, but brute-force attempts are no longer blocked. Starting it again reloads the jails; check the configuration before disabling it.
problems: An IP is banned by mistake — run `fail2ban-client status <jail>` and unban it with `fail2ban-client set <jail> unbanip <ip>`.
Fail2ban does not block attacks — check `fail2ban-client status` and the jail log path and filter.
The service will not start — run `fail2ban-client -t` and read the reported configuration error.

ufw.name: Uncomplicated Firewall
ufw.what: Manages a simple set of firewall rules with iptables or nftables.
ufw.ifFails: Firewall rules may not load or change. Check the rules and keep console access; a bad rule set can cut off remote access.
ufw.details: UFW is a front-end for iptables or nftables that makes firewall rules easier to manage. It stores its rules and enabled state in `/etc/ufw/`, and its rules are applied at boot. It is common on Ubuntu and can be installed on Debian. It only controls the host firewall, not the provider's external firewall.
ufw.stop: Stopping UFW does not necessarily remove the rules already loaded in the kernel; disabling it with `ufw disable` does. Either way, the server can become exposed or unreachable depending on the current rules. Keep console access and review the rules before changing the firewall.
problems: A service is unreachable — run `ufw status verbose` and allow the port if it is missing.
You are locked out after enabling the firewall — use the provider console and allow SSH before re-enabling UFW.
Rules do not survive a reboot — check that UFW is enabled and that its configuration was saved.

nftables.name: nftables firewall
nftables.what: The modern Linux packet filter used for firewall rules.
nftables.ifFails: Firewall rules may disappear or fail to load, leaving services exposed or unreachable. Check the ruleset and keep console access.
nftables.details: nftables is the modern Linux packet filter and the default firewall framework on current Debian releases. It reads rules from `/etc/nftables.conf` and applies them with the `nft` command. It can filter, translate addresses and count traffic. UFW and Docker may add their own rules alongside yours.
nftables.stop: Stopping nftables does not flush the rules already loaded in the kernel unless the unit's stop command does so. A reload applies the file again, and a bad ruleset can cut off remote access. Keep console access and validate the rules before reloading.
problems: The ruleset is empty after boot — check `/etc/nftables.conf` and whether `nftables.service` is enabled.
The server is unreachable after a change — use the console and check the input chain and SSH port.
Docker and nftables rules conflict — check `nft list ruleset` and Docker's firewall integration before adding rules.

iptables.name: iptables firewall
iptables.what: The legacy Linux firewall and its persistent rule loader.
iptables.ifFails: Firewall rules may be missing after a restart or reload. Check the saved rules and keep console access before changing them.
iptables.details: iptables is the traditional Linux packet filter. `netfilter-persistent` loads saved rules at boot, and `ip6tables` applies the IPv6 rules while `ipset` stores large address sets. These units keep the firewall active across reboots; they do not configure the rules for you.
iptables.stop: Stopping or disabling them can leave the firewall open or drop the saved rules after a reboot. That may expose services or cut off SSH. Keep console access and verify the saved rules before changing anything.
problems: Rules disappear after reboot — check `/etc/iptables/rules.v4` and run `netfilter-persistent save`.
SSH is blocked after a rule change — use the provider console and check `iptables -L -n -v`.
IPv6 traffic is not filtered — check `/etc/iptables/rules.v6` and `ip6tables -L`.

apparmor.name: AppArmor
apparmor.what: Restricts what programs can access with per-application security profiles.
apparmor.ifFails: New AppArmor profiles may not load and confined applications may fail to start. Check the kernel log and profiles before restarting.
apparmor.details: AppArmor confines programs with profiles that limit the files and capabilities they can use. It is enabled at boot and profiles are loaded from `/etc/apparmor.d/`. On Debian it often protects services such as web servers and databases. A profile can be in complain mode, which logs violations without blocking them.
apparmor.stop: Disabling AppArmor at boot, or unloading the profiles with `aa-teardown`, removes the confinement, so programs can access anything their user permissions allow. Services keep running, but the extra protection is gone. Reload profiles instead of disabling the service when you change them.
problems: A confined service fails after an update — check `aa-status` and the kernel log for `DENIED` lines, then update or disable the profile.
A profile will not load — run `apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/<profile>` and read the error.
AppArmor is not enforcing — check `aa-status` and whether the kernel command line disabled it.

auditd.name: Linux audit daemon
auditd.what: Records security-relevant system events for auditing.
auditd.ifFails: Security events stop being recorded. Check disk space and the audit rules before restarting; audit failures can affect compliance.
auditd.details: auditd records security-relevant events such as logins, file access and privilege changes according to rules in `/etc/audit/rules.d/`. It writes audit records to `/var/log/audit/audit.log` and can forward them to another system. It is used for compliance and incident investigation. It does not replace application logs.
auditd.stop: Stopping auditd stops new audit records from being written; the kernel may still generate events that are dropped. Existing logs remain. Do not leave it stopped on a system that requires auditing; check disk space and rules before restarting.
problems: Audit logs are not written — check `systemctl status auditd`, `auditctl -s` and free space in `/var/log/audit`.
The audit service will not start — check `journalctl -u auditd -n 50 --no-pager` and the rules in `/etc/audit/rules.d/`.
The log fills the disk — check `auditctl -s`, rotate `/var/log/audit/audit.log` and review the rules.

polkit.name: PolicyKit
polkit.what: Controls whether users and services may perform privileged system actions.
polkit.ifFails: Graphical or service tools may be unable to authorize privileged operations. Check the logs; restarting can interrupt active sessions.
polkit.details: PolicyKit, now often called polkit, decides whether a user or service may perform a privileged action. Applications ask polkit instead of running as root, and polkit checks the action rules and the user's session. Its rules live in `/usr/share/polkit-1/actions/` and `/etc/polkit-1/rules.d/`. It is common on desktops and on servers managed through graphical or D-Bus tools.
polkit.stop: Stopping polkit prevents new authorization requests from being answered, so tools that need it may fail. Existing processes keep running. Restarting can interrupt active sessions; check the logs and the rules before changing it.
problems: A tool says authorization is not available — check `systemctl status polkit` and `journalctl -u polkit -n 50 --no-pager`.
A user cannot perform an action — check the action ID with `pkaction` and the rules in `/etc/polkit-1/rules.d/`.
Polkit does not start — check the D-Bus system bus and the polkit logs.

qemu-guest-agent.name: QEMU guest agent
qemu-guest-agent.what: Lets the virtual machine host query and control this guest.
qemu-guest-agent.ifFails: The host cannot query the guest or run graceful shutdown and snapshot commands. Check the virtio channel; it is not needed by most services.
qemu-guest-agent.details: The QEMU guest agent runs inside a virtual machine and talks to the host over a virtio serial channel. It lets the host query the guest, freeze filesystems for snapshots and request a graceful shutdown. It is useful only in a virtual machine managed by QEMU/KVM or a platform that supports it. It does not affect normal services on the guest.
qemu-guest-agent.stop: Stopping the agent removes those host controls, but the guest keeps running normally. Snapshot and shutdown requests from the host may fail or fall back to a hard power-off. It is safe to stop if you do not use host-side guest management.
problems: The host says the agent is not running — check `systemctl status qemu-guest-agent` and that the virtio serial device exists.
Shutdown or snapshot commands fail — check the agent logs and the host's guest agent configuration.
The agent is not installed — install `qemu-guest-agent` in the guest; it is separate from the QEMU host packages.

cloud-init.name: Cloud-init
cloud-init.what: Configures a cloud instance on first boot, including users, SSH keys and networking.
cloud-init.ifFails: Provisioning or later configuration steps can fail on the next boot. Check its logs and configuration; avoid rerunning it blindly on a live server.
cloud-init.details: Cloud-init configures a cloud instance during first boot: users, SSH keys, networking, packages and files. It reads metadata from the provider and configuration from `/etc/cloud/` and `/var/lib/cloud/`. It normally runs once per boot stage and then marks the instance as configured. Later boots can still run user-data scripts (customisation scripts supplied by the provider or administrator) if configured.
cloud-init.stop: Stopping cloud-init does not undo the configuration already applied. It may prevent later stages or user-data scripts from running, so a reboot could leave the instance partially configured. Disable specific modules or data sources instead of stopping it blindly.
problems: A new instance has no SSH key or user — check `cloud-init status --long` and the provider's user-data and metadata.
Cloud-init fails on boot — read `/var/log/cloud-init.log` and `/var/log/cloud-init-output.log`.
Cloud-init runs again and changes the system — check `/var/lib/cloud/` and the cloud-init configuration for repeated modules.

snapd.name: Snap daemon
snapd.what: Installs and updates snap packages and their services.
snapd.ifFails: Snap applications may stop updating or start. Check the snapd logs; if you do not use snaps, it can stay stopped.
snapd.details: snapd installs, updates and runs snap packages. It mounts squashfs images, manages snap services and refreshes them automatically. Snap data lives under `/var/snap/`, and the packages are mounted under `/snap/`. It is optional on Debian; servers that do not use snaps can run without it.
snapd.stop: Stopping snapd stops automatic refreshes and may affect running snap services, though already running applications can continue for a while. Snap commands fail until it returns. If you do not use snaps, it is safe to leave it disabled.
problems: A snap application does not start — check `systemctl status snapd` and `snap version`.
Snaps do not update — check `snap refresh --time` and the snapd log.
Snapd uses too much disk — run `snap list --all` and remove old revisions with `snap set system refresh.retain=2`.

modemmanager.name: ModemManager
modemmanager.what: Detects and manages mobile broadband modems.
modemmanager.ifFails: Mobile broadband connections may not be configured or reconnected. It is optional on servers without a modem.
modemmanager.details: ModemManager detects mobile broadband modems and exposes them to NetworkManager or other connection tools. It handles SIM state, signal information and connection setup. It is useful on laptops and routers with a cellular modem; most servers do not have one. It does not manage Ethernet or Wi-Fi.
modemmanager.stop: Stopping ModemManager leaves existing modem connections alone for a while but prevents new ones from being configured or reconnected. It is safe to disable on a server without a cellular modem. Check whether NetworkManager expects it before removing it.
problems: A modem is not detected — run `mmcli -L` and check `journalctl -u modemmanager -n 50 --no-pager`.
The connection does not come up — check the SIM state with `mmcli -m 0` and the NetworkManager connection profile.
ModemManager conflicts with another tool — check which service manages the modem and disable the one you do not use.

wpa-supplicant.name: WPA supplicant
wpa-supplicant.what: Connects the machine to protected Wi-Fi networks.
wpa-supplicant.ifFails: A Wi-Fi connection may drop or fail to reconnect. Keep wired or console access; check the Wi-Fi configuration before restarting.
wpa-supplicant.details: wpa_supplicant connects a Wi-Fi interface to WPA/WPA2/WPA3 networks. It reads configuration from `/etc/wpa_supplicant/` and is often started by ifupdown, NetworkManager or a systemd unit. It handles authentication and roaming, but not IP addresses. Servers usually use Ethernet and do not need it.
wpa-supplicant.stop: Stopping wpa_supplicant disconnects the Wi-Fi interface it manages, and remote access over that link ends. Other interfaces keep working. Keep console access and check the configuration before restarting; NetworkManager may restart it automatically.
problems: Wi-Fi does not connect — run `wpa_cli status` and check the network block in `/etc/wpa_supplicant/wpa_supplicant.conf`.
The connection drops repeatedly — check signal strength with `iw dev` and the supplicant log in the journal.
Wrong password or key — update the network block with `wpa_passphrase` and reload the interface.

avahi.name: Avahi
avahi.what: Advertises services on the local network with mDNS/DNS-SD.
avahi.ifFails: Local discovery of printers or services may stop. This is usually optional on a server; check the logs if you rely on it.

cups.name: CUPS printing
cups.what: Runs the local printing service and print queues.
cups.ifFails: Printing and print queues stop working. It is optional on servers; check the logs if this machine manages printers.
cups.details: CUPS runs local print queues and shares printers on the network. `cups-browsed` discovers printers advertised on the local network. Servers rarely need printing, so these units are optional unless the machine manages printers.
cups.stop: Stopping CUPS stops print jobs and shared printers. Local documents are not affected. It is safe to disable it on a server that does not print.
problems: Nothing prints — check `systemctl status cups` and the queue with `lpstat -p -d`.
The printer disappears — check `cups-browsed`, the network and the printer address.
CUPS fails to start — read `journalctl -u cups -n 50 --no-pager` and check `/etc/cups/cupsd.conf`.

bluetooth.name: Bluetooth service
bluetooth.ifFails: Bluetooth devices cannot connect. It is optional on most servers and can usually stay stopped.

mariadb.name: MariaDB / MySQL
mariadb.what: A relational database server used by many web applications.
mariadb.ifFails: Applications lose their database and may return errors or stop. Check disk space and logs before restarting; a restart cuts every open connection, so do it when the applications can tolerate a short outage.

mysql.name: MySQL
mysql.ifFails: Applications lose their database and may return errors or stop. Check disk space and logs before restarting; a restart cuts every open connection, so do it when the applications can tolerate a short outage.

postgresql.name: PostgreSQL
postgresql.what: A relational database server known for reliability and SQL features.
postgresql.ifFails: Applications lose their database and may return errors or stop. Check disk space and logs before restarting; a restart cuts every open connection, so do it when the applications can tolerate a short outage.

redis.name: Redis
redis.what: An in-memory data store used for caching, queues and sessions.
redis.ifFails: Caches and sessions can disappear or writes can fail. Check memory and persistence logs; restart only after deciding whether losing volatile data is acceptable.

valkey.name: Valkey
valkey.what: An open-source in-memory data store compatible with Redis.
valkey.ifFails: Caches and sessions can disappear or writes can fail. Check memory and persistence logs; restart only after deciding whether losing volatile data is acceptable.

memcached.name: Memcached
memcached.what: A small in-memory cache used to speed up applications.
memcached.ifFails: The cache is lost and applications fall back to their slower data source. It is usually safe to restart, but sessions stored there may be lost.

mongodb.name: MongoDB
mongodb.what: A document database that stores JSON-like records.
mongodb.ifFails: Applications lose their database and may return errors or stop. Check disk space, logs and replica set health before restarting.

rabbitmq.name: RabbitMQ
rabbitmq.what: A message broker that queues jobs and events between services.
rabbitmq.ifFails: Messages may queue up and workers stop receiving jobs. Check disk space, memory and the management UI before restarting.

php-fpm.name: PHP-FPM
php-fpm.what: Runs PHP web applications for a web server such as Nginx or Apache.
php-fpm.ifFails: PHP sites return errors or stop answering. Check the pool configuration and PHP logs before restarting.

wireguard.name: WireGuard VPN
wireguard.what: A fast VPN tunnel used for remote access or connecting networks.
wireguard.ifFails: VPN peers lose the tunnel and may lose access to private services. Check the interface configuration and keys; restarting drops active connections.

tailscale.name: Tailscale
tailscale.what: Connects this machine to a private Tailscale network.
tailscale.ifFails: The machine disappears from the tailnet and remote access through it stops. Check authentication and network access before restarting.

openvpn.name: OpenVPN
openvpn.what: A VPN server or client that provides encrypted network access.
openvpn.ifFails: VPN clients lose their tunnel and remote services may become unreachable. Check the configuration and logs; restarting drops active connections.

bind9.name: BIND DNS server
bind9.what: An authoritative and recursive DNS server.
bind9.ifFails: DNS resolution can fail for everything that depends on it. Validate the configuration with named-checkconf and check logs before restarting.

unbound.name: Unbound DNS resolver
unbound.ifFails: Name resolution can fail for local clients and services. Check the configuration and logs; a bad config prevents it from starting.

dnsmasq.name: Dnsmasq
dnsmasq.what: A small DNS forwarder and DHCP server for local networks.
dnsmasq.ifFails: Local DNS or DHCP can stop, and clients may lose addresses or name resolution. Check the configuration and logs before restarting.

smartd.name: S.M.A.R.T. monitoring
smartd.what: Warns about failing disks using their S.M.A.R.T. health data.
smartd.ifFails: Disk health warnings may not be sent. It is optional, but check the logs and start it again if you rely on disk monitoring.

lvm2.name: LVM
lvm2.what: Manages logical volumes and snapshots on top of physical disks.
lvm2.ifFails: Logical volumes may not activate and filesystems can become unavailable. Check the LVM logs and disk state; do not force changes without a backup.

mdmonitor.name: Linux software RAID
mdmonitor.what: Monitors and manages md RAID arrays.
mdmonitor.ifFails: Array problems may go unnoticed and degraded arrays may not be repaired. Check /proc/mdstat and the logs before restarting.

zfs.name: OpenZFS
zfs.what: Manages ZFS pools, datasets, snapshots and scrubs.
zfs.ifFails: ZFS datasets may become unavailable and pool problems may go unnoticed. Check zpool status and the logs; never force-import a damaged pool.

talaia-agent.name: Talaia agent
talaia-agent.what: Connects this server to Talaia and runs the actions requested from the panel.
talaia-agent.ifFails: The server appears offline in Talaia and cannot be managed from the panel. Check the agent logs and its connection to the core before restarting.
talaia-agent.details: talaia-agent connects outbound to the Talaia core and runs typed actions on this server. It reports inventory and health, and keeps the connection open so the panel can manage the host. It is not needed on the core machine unless that machine is also managed.
talaia-agent.stop: Stopping talaia-agent makes the server appear offline and stops panel actions on it. Containers and services keep running. Start it again after checking its configuration and the core connection.
problems: The server shows offline — check `systemctl status talaia-agent` and `journalctl -u talaia-agent -n 50 --no-pager`.
Enrollment fails — check the core URL and CA fingerprint in `/etc/talaia/agent.toml`.
Actions time out — check the agent-to-core connection and the core logs.

talaia-hostd.name: Talaia update helper
talaia-hostd.what: Runs the root script that lets the Talaia panel update the core safely.
talaia-hostd.ifFails: The panel may not apply updates or may need to be updated from the host.
talaia-hostd.details: talaia-hostd is not a systemd service: it is the root script `/usr/local/sbin/talaia-hostd` installed by the Talaia installer. The core cannot touch Docker; it writes the requested commit to `/var/lib/talaia-host/requests/update.json`, and `talaia-update.path` starts the one-shot `talaia-update.service`, which runs `talaia-hostd update`; progress goes to `/var/lib/talaia-host/status.json` and the panel shows it in Settings > System. That script accepts only a commit on `origin/main` newer than the current one, backs up the database, fast-forwards the clone, rebuilds the Docker stack and waits for `/healthz`; if the new core does not answer, it returns to the previous commit and restores the backup. It exists only on the server that runs `talaia-core`; its configuration is `/etc/talaia/hostd.conf`, and `talaia-update.service` being inactive between updates is normal.
talaia-hostd.stop: Stopping `talaia-update.service` when no update is running is normal and does nothing; the unit is inactive between updates. Stopping or disabling `talaia-update.path` prevents new update requests from being picked up. Keep it enabled on the core server, and use Settings > System to see whether an update is running or failed.
problems: An update stays queued — check `systemctl status talaia-update.path`, make sure it is enabled and look for the request in `/var/lib/talaia-host/requests/update.json`.
An update failed or was rolled back — read `journalctl -u talaia-update -n 100 --no-pager` and the log in Settings > System.
The helper is missing — the core may have been installed with `--no-hostd`; reinstall the core without that option or install the helper on the host.

talaia-core.name: Talaia core
talaia-core.what: The Talaia server that stores data, serves the panel and coordinates agents.
talaia-core.ifFails: The panel and agent connections stop working. Check the database and core logs before restarting, and keep a backup of its data.
talaia-core.details: talaia-core is the central Talaia service: API, panel, database access, agent hub, jobs and alerts. It is normally run by Docker Compose rather than as a host systemd service, so this unit may not exist on every installation. When present, it starts the core and its dependencies.
talaia-core.stop: Stopping talaia-core takes down the panel and cuts agent connections. Agents reconnect and containers keep running, but no management works until it returns. Keep a database backup and use the packaged service manager when possible.
problems: The panel does not open — check `systemctl status talaia-core` and the core logs.
Agents cannot connect — check the public hostname, ports and the agent port certificate.
The core fails after an update — check the database migration log and restore the previous version if needed.

httpd.name: Apache HTTP Server image
httpd.what: Serves websites and static files from a container.
httpd.ifFails: The web service in this container stops answering. Check the container logs and its mounted configuration before restarting.

traefik.name: Traefik
traefik.what: A reverse proxy and load balancer that discovers container services.
traefik.ifFails: Routes to containers may stop working and certificates may not renew. Check its logs, providers and routing labels before restarting.

nginx-proxy-manager.name: Nginx Proxy Manager
nginx-proxy-manager.what: A web UI that manages Nginx reverse proxies and TLS certificates.
nginx-proxy-manager.ifFails: Proxied sites or certificate renewal may stop. Check its logs and database; keep a backup of its configuration.

portainer.name: Portainer
portainer.what: A web interface for managing Docker containers, images and stacks.
portainer.ifFails: The Docker management UI becomes unavailable, but running containers continue. Check its data volume and logs before restarting.

portainer-agent.name: Portainer agent
portainer-agent.what: Lets a Portainer server manage the Docker host it runs on.
portainer-agent.ifFails: Portainer can no longer manage this Docker host. Check its connection and logs; running containers are not affected.

watchtower.name: Watchtower
watchtower.what: Periodically updates running containers when their images change.
watchtower.ifFails: Containers stop being updated automatically. Check its logs and schedule; it is optional if you update images another way.

grafana.name: Grafana
grafana.what: Builds dashboards and graphs from metrics, logs and other data sources.
grafana.ifFails: Dashboards and alerts in Grafana stop loading. Check its database and data source connections before restarting.

prometheus.name: Prometheus
prometheus.what: Collects and stores time-series metrics and evaluates alert rules.
prometheus.ifFails: Metrics stop being collected and alert rules stop firing. Check disk space, its configuration and the targets; restart only after checking the WAL state.

node-exporter.name: Prometheus Node Exporter
node-exporter.what: Exposes CPU, memory, disk and network metrics of the host.
node-exporter.ifFails: Host metrics disappear from dashboards and alerts. Check its logs and port; restarting it does not affect the host services.

cadvisor.name: cAdvisor
cadvisor.what: Collects resource usage metrics from Docker containers.
cadvisor.ifFails: Container metrics disappear from dashboards and alerts. Check its logs and access to the Docker socket before restarting.

loki.name: Grafana Loki
loki.what: Stores and queries logs in a compact, label-based store.
loki.ifFails: Log search and log-based alerts stop working; new logs may be dropped. Check disk space and its configuration before restarting.

promtail.name: Grafana Promtail
promtail.what: Ships logs from the host or containers to Grafana Loki.
promtail.ifFails: New logs stop reaching Loki, but the applications keep running. Check its configuration and connection to Loki before restarting.

wordpress.name: WordPress
wordpress.what: Publishes websites and blogs and stores their content in a database.
wordpress.ifFails: The site returns errors or stops loading. Check the container logs, database connection and disk space before restarting.

nextcloud.name: Nextcloud
nextcloud.what: Provides private file sync, sharing and collaboration.
nextcloud.ifFails: Users cannot sync or open files. Check the database, data volume and logs before restarting; do not delete the data volume.

gitea.name: Gitea
gitea.what: A self-hosted Git service for repositories, issues and pull requests.
gitea.ifFails: Git access and the web interface stop working. Check its database, repositories volume and logs before restarting.

vaultwarden.name: Vaultwarden
vaultwarden.what: A lightweight Bitwarden-compatible password manager server.
vaultwarden.ifFails: Password clients cannot sync or log in. Check its database and logs before restarting; keep a backup of the data volume.

minio.name: MinIO
minio.what: An S3-compatible object storage server for files and backups.
minio.ifFails: Applications and backups cannot read or write objects. Check disk space, the data volumes and cluster health before restarting.

adminer.name: Adminer
adminer.what: A small web interface for managing SQL databases.
adminer.ifFails: The database web interface is unavailable, but the databases keep running. Check its logs and network access before restarting.

phpmyadmin.name: phpMyAdmin
phpmyadmin.what: A web interface for managing MySQL and MariaDB databases.
phpmyadmin.ifFails: The database web interface is unavailable, but the databases keep running. Check its web server, PHP and database connection before restarting.

pgadmin.name: pgAdmin
pgadmin.what: A web interface for managing PostgreSQL databases.
pgadmin.ifFails: The PostgreSQL web interface is unavailable, but the databases keep running. Check its data volume and database connection before restarting.

uptime-kuma.name: Uptime Kuma
uptime-kuma.what: Monitors websites and services and sends downtime notifications.
uptime-kuma.ifFails: Monitoring and downtime alerts stop. Check its data volume and logs; uptime checks resume when it starts again.

pihole.name: Pi-hole
pihole.what: A DNS sinkhole and local DNS server that blocks advertising domains.
pihole.ifFails: Clients using it lose DNS and may lose internet access. Check its configuration and upstream DNS; keep another resolver available if possible.

adguard.name: AdGuard Home
adguard.what: A DNS server that filters ads and tracking for the local network.
adguard.ifFails: Clients using it lose DNS and may lose internet access. Check its configuration and upstream DNS; keep another resolver available if possible.

certbot.name: Certbot
certbot.what: Obtains and renews TLS certificates from Let's Encrypt.
certbot.ifFails: Certificates may expire and HTTPS sites will show errors. Check its logs, DNS and port 80/443 access; run it manually only after fixing the cause.
certbot.details: Certbot asks Let's Encrypt for the TLS certificates that make HTTPS work and installs them in the web server. A timer usually runs it every day, so sites renew without anyone visiting them. The service performs one renewal pass; the timer is what makes it repeat.
certbot.stop: Stopping Certbot stops automatic renewals. Existing certificates keep working until they expire, and then browsers show security errors and some clients refuse the connection. Do not disable it unless another tool renews the same certificates.
problems: A domain no longer points to this server (it moved to another host or its DNS record was removed), so the HTTP challenge fails every day — remove that certificate here with `certbot delete --cert-name <domain>` and disable its old web site configuration.

Port 80 is closed, redirected by the firewall or taken by another proxy, so the HTTP challenge cannot be reached — open port 80 for the challenge or switch Certbot to DNS validation, then run `certbot renew --dry-run`.
The web server configuration is broken or the certificate files were moved — fix `apachectl configtest` or `nginx -t`, restore the expected paths and run `certbot renew --dry-run`.

registry.name: Docker registry
registry.what: Stores and serves Docker images for pulls and pushes.
registry.ifFails: Image pulls and pushes fail, and deployments that need new images stop. Check disk space, authentication and the storage backend before restarting.

anacron.name: Anacron
anacron.what: Runs daily, weekly and monthly maintenance jobs on machines that are not always on.
anacron.ifFails: Scheduled maintenance jobs may not run after the server has been off. Check its logs if backups, log rotation or cleanup stop happening.
anacron.details: Anacron complements cron: it remembers when daily, weekly or monthly jobs last ran and starts them after boot if their time was missed. On a server it usually runs the jobs in `/etc/cron.daily`, `/etc/cron.weekly` and `/etc/cron.monthly`. It is useful on laptops and on servers that are not powered all the time.
anacron.stop: Stopping anacron means missed maintenance jobs are not caught up after boot. The jobs run by cron may still run while the machine is on, but daily tasks can be delayed. It is usually safe only if cron and another scheduler cover the same work.
problems: A maintenance job did not run — check `/var/spool/anacron` for the last-run timestamps and read the unit log with `journalctl -u anacron -n 50 --no-pager`.
A job runs at the wrong time — anacron starts after boot and then waits for its configured delay; check `/etc/anacrontab` and the job's own schedule.
The service is masked or disabled — check `systemctl status anacron` and enable it again if you rely on catch-up jobs.

logrotate.name: Logrotate
logrotate.what: Rotates, compresses and removes old log files so disks do not fill up.
logrotate.ifFails: Log files keep growing and can fill the disk; some services may stop writing or the server may become unstable.
logrotate.details: Logrotate checks its configuration regularly, often through a systemd timer, and renames or compresses logs when they reach a size or age limit. It can also tell a service to reopen its log file after rotation. Configuration lives in `/etc/logrotate.conf` and `/etc/logrotate.d`.
logrotate.stop: Stopping logrotate leaves old logs in place and new entries keep growing the same files. A full disk can then break services and the panel. Keep it running and fix configuration errors instead of disabling it.
problems: Logs are not rotating — run `logrotate --debug /etc/logrotate.conf` and check the timer with `systemctl status logrotate.timer`.
A log is huge or the disk is full — inspect `/etc/logrotate.d` for the service's rules and rotate that file manually with `logrotate -f /etc/logrotate.conf`.
A service keeps writing to the old file — add the correct `postrotate` command to make the service reopen its log, then test with `logrotate --debug`.

man-db.name: Manual page index
man-db.what: Builds the index and cache used by the `man` command.
man-db.ifFails: Manual pages may be missing from searches or `man` may show an old version after packages change.
man-db.details: The man-db service runs `mandb` to rebuild the manual page index after packages install or remove documentation. It uses a systemd timer or package triggers, so it normally works in the background. Without it, `man` can still open a page by path but searches and the whatis database may be stale.
man-db.stop: Stopping it only skips index updates; existing manual pages remain available. It is safe to leave it off for a while, but after installing or removing packages `man -k` may miss pages. Run `mandb` by hand once if you need the index.
problems: `man -k` finds nothing — run `mandb` and check `systemctl status man-db` and its timer.
A manual page is missing — confirm the package installed its man page under `/usr/share/man` and rebuild the index with `mandb`.
The service fails with permission errors — check free disk space and the log with `journalctl -u man-db -n 50 --no-pager`.

dpkg-db-backup.name: Package database backup
dpkg-db-backup.what: Saves a daily backup of the dpkg package database.
dpkg-db-backup.ifFails: A damaged package database cannot be restored from a recent automatic copy.
dpkg-db-backup.details: The service copies the files that record installed packages, versions and package status to `/var/backups`. It runs once a day and keeps a few recent copies, so the package manager can be repaired if its database is damaged. It does not back up your application data.
dpkg-db-backup.stop: Stopping it only stops these package-database copies; installed software keeps working. It is safe for a short time, but you lose a simple recovery point for dpkg. Keep it enabled on normal servers.
problems: No recent backup exists — check `systemctl status dpkg-db-backup` and the timer, and inspect `/var/backups` for `dpkg.*` files.
The disk is full — remove old backups you no longer need, but keep at least the latest copy.
The service fails — check `journalctl -u dpkg-db-backup -n 50 --no-pager` for permission or disk errors.

e2scrub.name: ext4 online check
e2scrub.what: Checks ext4 filesystems for metadata errors while they are online.
e2scrub.ifFails: Filesystem errors may go unnoticed until they cause data loss.
e2scrub.details: e2scrub runs on ext4 filesystems that use LVM and checks a read-only snapshot for metadata problems. It is a light check, not a replacement for a full offline fsck. A timer runs it regularly, usually once a week.
e2scrub.stop: Stopping it stops these online checks; the filesystem continues working normally. It is safe to disable on machines without LVM ext4 filesystems, but errors may then be found only by a manual check. Do not run a full fsck on a mounted filesystem.
problems: The timer fails — check `systemctl status e2scrub_all.timer` and `journalctl -u e2scrub_all -n 50 --no-pager`.
No snapshot is created — e2scrub needs LVM free space; check `lvs` and free extents in the volume group.
Errors are reported — do not ignore them; plan an offline `e2fsck -f` after unmounting the filesystem.

fstrim.name: SSD trim
fstrim.what: Tells an SSD which blocks are no longer used.
fstrim.ifFails: The SSD may keep erased blocks longer and write performance or lifetime can suffer.
fstrim.details: fstrim sends TRIM requests for free blocks on mounted filesystems. A timer runs it weekly on supported SSDs, so the drive can erase unused blocks in advance. It does not delete your files and does not run on filesystems that do not support TRIM.
fstrim.stop: Stopping the timer only skips the automatic TRIM; data and mounts are unaffected. You can run `fstrim --all` by hand later. It is usually safe to disable on virtual disks that do not support discard.
problems: The timer is missing — check `systemctl status fstrim.timer` and enable it if the disk supports TRIM.
fstrim reports `discard operation not supported` — the filesystem or virtual disk does not support discard; no action is needed unless the provider supports it.
TRIM takes too long — check the disk health and avoid running it during busy hours.

phpsessionclean.name: PHP session cleanup
phpsessionclean.what: Deletes old PHP session files from the session directory.
phpsessionclean.ifFails: Old session files can fill the disk, and expired sessions may be kept longer than intended.
phpsessionclean.details: PHP stores sessions in a directory such as `/var/lib/php/sessions`, and old files are not removed by every request. This timer runs a cleanup script that removes expired sessions according to the PHP settings. It matters only on servers that run PHP applications with file-based sessions.
phpsessionclean.stop: Stopping it leaves expired session files on disk; active sessions are not affected. It is safe for a short time, but the directory can grow and fill the disk. Run the cleanup script by hand if you disable it.
problems: The sessions directory grows — inspect `session.save_path` in `php.ini` and the cleanup timer, and remove only files that are clearly expired.
Users are logged out unexpectedly — check the PHP `session.gc_maxlifetime` setting; cleanup may be removing sessions earlier than the application expects.
The timer fails — check `systemctl status phpsessionclean.timer` and the service log.

sshd-keygen.name: SSH host key generator
sshd-keygen.what: Creates the SSH host keys the server uses on its first boot.
sshd-keygen.ifFails: SSH clients may reject the server identity or refuse to connect, especially after the host keys were removed.
sshd-keygen.details: The service creates missing SSH host key pairs in `/etc/ssh` during the first boot of a Debian system. These keys identify the server to clients and are not the same as your personal login keys. It runs once and does nothing when the keys already exist.
sshd-keygen.stop: Stopping it does not remove existing host keys and does not affect running SSH connections. It is safe when the keys already exist, but a fresh machine can fail to start SSH if the keys were never generated. Generate them with `ssh-keygen -A` if needed.
problems: SSH refuses connections after a rebuild — check that host keys exist in `/etc/ssh` and run `ssh-keygen -A`.
Clients warn that the host key changed — this can be expected after reinstalling; verify the new fingerprint before accepting it.
The service fails at boot — check `systemctl status sshd-keygen` and the logs; permissions or a full disk may prevent key creation.

uuidd.name: UUID daemon
uuidd.what: Generates UUIDs for programs that need unique identifiers.
uuidd.ifFails: Some applications may fall back to slower or less reliable UUID generation.
uuidd.details: uuidd is a small daemon that produces universally unique identifiers on request. It exists so many processes can get UUIDs without each one generating them from the same random source. Most servers only use it when a package asks for it.
uuidd.stop: Stopping uuidd is usually harmless: programs that need a UUID can generate one themselves. It may affect applications that explicitly require the service. It is safe to leave stopped if nothing on the server uses it.
problems: A service cannot get a UUID — check `systemctl status uuidd` and start it.
The socket is missing — check `systemctl status uuidd.socket`; systemd usually starts the daemon on demand.
The daemon fails after a reboot — check `journalctl -u uuidd -n 50 --no-pager` and the `/run` filesystem.

rc-local.name: Local boot commands
rc-local.what: Runs the commands in `/etc/rc.local` during boot.
rc-local.ifFails: Custom startup commands in that file do not run after a reboot.
rc-local.details: rc-local is a compatibility unit for administrators who still use `/etc/rc.local` instead of a native systemd service. On Debian it usually runs late in the boot, after the network and local filesystems are ready. It only matters if that file exists and contains commands.
rc-local.stop: Stopping or disabling it means `/etc/rc.local` is not executed at boot. The rest of the system continues normally. It is safe if you no longer use that file or have moved its commands to a proper service.
problems: Commands in `/etc/rc.local` do not run — make sure the file is executable and check `systemctl status rc-local`.
Boot waits or fails — read `journalctl -u rc-local -b` and make the commands exit successfully.
The unit is masked — check `systemctl status rc-local`; enable it only if you rely on that file.

grub.name: GRUB bootloader
grub.what: Updates the bootloader configuration and keeps the GRUB boot menu ready.
grub.ifFails: The server may fail to boot or boot an old kernel after a kernel or configuration change.
grub.details: The grub-common unit runs `update-grub` when the kernel or boot configuration changes, so the boot menu lists the right kernels. It does not install kernels itself. A failed update can leave the boot menu stale, so check it after kernel upgrades.
grub.stop: Stopping it only prevents automatic menu regeneration; an existing menu keeps working. The next kernel update may not appear at boot. Generate it manually with `update-grub` if you have disabled it.
problems: The server boots an old kernel — run `update-grub` and check `/boot` for free space.
The unit fails — read `journalctl -u grub-common -n 50 --no-pager` and fix the reported configuration.
The boot menu is missing an entry — confirm the kernel package is installed and regenerate the menu.

rescue-mode.name: Rescue mode
rescue-mode.what: Provides the emergency and rescue boot targets for repairing a broken system.
rescue-mode.ifFails: A serious boot problem may leave you without the minimal recovery shell.
rescue-mode.details: The emergency and rescue targets are special systemd states used when normal boot fails. Rescue mode starts a small system with local filesystems and a root shell; emergency mode starts even less. They are not meant to run during normal operation.
rescue-mode.stop: You cannot normally stop these targets in a healthy session; they are selected at boot. Disabling or masking them removes a recovery path, so do not do it. Use them only when the normal boot cannot complete.
problems: The server drops into rescue mode — check the boot log with `journalctl -xb` and fix the failed mount or service.
Rescue mode asks for the root password — use the root password or boot from the provider's console or rescue image.
The system cannot reach emergency mode — use the provider recovery console or a live image.

initrd.name: Initial RAM disk
initrd.what: Builds the temporary initramfs image used during early boot.
initrd.ifFails: The server may fail to mount its root filesystem or load the drivers needed to boot.
initrd.details: initrd units regenerate the initramfs after kernel or storage driver changes. The initramfs contains the modules and scripts needed before the real root filesystem is mounted. Debian runs this automatically after kernel package updates.
initrd.stop: Stopping the generator does not affect the current boot or an existing initramfs. A later kernel may boot without the right drivers. Regenerate it with `update-initramfs -u` after fixing the cause.
